Sources indicate that begin with just a few minutes each day. Even a short period of meditation can have significant benefits, and starting small makes the practice feel more manageable. As you become more comfortable with the process, you can gradually extend your meditation time.

💙 Begin your meditation journey with Jeff Warren in this Meditation for Beginners series.

According to recent reports, meditation is a personal experience, and there’s no single "right" way to do it. Many people form expectations based on others' descriptions, but each person's meditation journey is unique. You don’t need to empty your mind or feel bliss in every session. Notice your thoughts and feelings without judgment, and meet whatever comes up with kindness and curiosity.

💙 Explore how having Expectations can affect us and our lives with Tamara Levitt on the Daily Calm.

Physical discomfort can be a distraction during meditation. To help settle your body and prepare for stillness, consider some gentle stretching or mindful movement, such as yoga or tai chi, before you begin. This can help release tension in the body and allow you to sit more comfortably.

💙 Follow along with The Daily Move’s Releasing Stress session to help you unwind before settling down.

Guided meditations, available through apps, websites, or local classes, can provide verbal instructions and cues to lead you through the meditation process. They can introduce you to different types of meditation, help keep your focus, and offer insights into how to handle common challenges like wandering thoughts or restlessness.

💙 Try this guided meditation to help you with Reframing Difficult Thoughts whenever your thoughts start to overwhelm you.

Sources indicate that it’s normal to encounter challenges as you begin your meditation practice. You might miss a day or find your mind wandering constantly. When this happens, treat yourself with kindness and compassion. Each time you notice your mind has drifted and come back to the present moment, you’re practicing.

💙 Practice this Loving Kindness meditation to guide you in cultivating feelings of kindness toward yourself and others.

Join a meditation group or find a community of practitioners that can provide support and a sense of connection. Sharing experiences with others on a similar path can be incredibly encouraging.

There’s no single agreed list, but these three approaches are often used to sort the many types of meditation:.

Concentration meditation: You rest your attention on a single point of reference, such as the breath, a mantra, a sound, or a candle flame. When your mind wanders, you return to it.

Sources indicate that mindfulness meditation: You widen your awareness to include thoughts, sensations, and your surroundings as they arise. It is often taught as part of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR).

Loving-kindness meditation (Metta): You build goodwill and warmth toward others, starting with yourself.

The idea of levels in meditation can vary depending on the tradition or practice. A way to think of meditation depth might include the different types and states.

Physical relaxation: The initial stage where the body relaxes deeply.

Concentration: The mind begins to focus, reducing distractions.

Mindful awareness: A state of heightened awareness of the present moment.

Deepening peace: Inner silence becomes more profound.

Insight: Understanding about yourself and reality may arise.

Blissful states: Experiences of joy or profound contentment.

Transcendence: A sense of unity or oneness with all, often considered the deepest level of meditation.

It has been revealed that the power of a meditation practice can vary from person to person, depending on individual needs, preferences, and goals. Some may find mindfulness meditation helpful for managing stress and enhancing self-awareness, while others prefer the structured approach of Transcendental Meditation or the heart-opening practices of loving-kindness meditation.

In a recent development, ultimately, the most ‘powerful’ type is the one you’ll keep practicing. Try a few to see which fits.

What is EMDR therapy, and does it actually work?

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Sources indicate that maybe a friend swears EMDR helped her move past something she’d carried for years.
  • It has been revealed that if you’re uncertain, that’s understandable, because EMDR can sound unconventional: you briefly recall a painful memory while following side-to-side stimulation, like tracking a moving target with your eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Sources indicate that maybe a friend swears EMDR helped her move past something she’d carried for years. Or maybe you came across it online while searching for ways to cope with a memory that still feels heavy. Whether you’ve heard of EMDR but don’t know how it works, or you’re familiar with the approach but skeptical, we’re here to break it all down.

It has been revealed that if you’re uncertain, that’s understandable, because EMDR can sound unconventional: you briefly recall a painful memory while following side-to-side stimulation, like tracking a moving target with your eyes. But the research tells a more reassuring story. It’s a well-studied therapy for trauma, and it’s increasingly explored for anxiety and depression, too.

Here’s what EMDR involves, what the research shows, and what a session is like, so you have a clearer picture of whether it might make sense for you.

Recent findings suggest that EMDR stands for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. It’s a structured therapy that helps the brain reprocess distressing memories so they carry less emotional weight. Psychologist Francine Shapiro, PhD, developed it in the late 1980s after she noticed that certain eye movements seemed to ease her own troubling thoughts.

It has been revealed that EMDR rests on Shapiro’s adaptive information processing model. The idea is that your brain normally files an experience away, so you can recall it later without feeling like you’re living it again. But a frightening or painful event can interrupt that process, leaving the memory raw and unfiled, still carrying the fear and detail of that moment. That’s why it can resurface later, as vivid as the day it happened.

Sources indicate that according to this model, “processing” a memory means helping your brain finish the filing. You don’t forget what happened, and the facts don’t change. What changes is the emotional charge it carries, so recalling it feels less like reliving it and more like remembering it. To help that happen, EMDR uses a technique called “bilateral stimulation.”.

EMDR uses a technique called bilateral stimulation. While you hold a difficult memory in mind, a trained therapist guides you through side-to-side stimulation.

Bilateral stimulation can take a few forms:.

eye movements that follow your therapist’s fingers.

gentle taps that switch between your hands or knees.

tones that play in one ear, then the other.

Sources indicate that there’s a theory behind the side-to-side part, though researchers are still working out exactly why it helps. The leading explanation is about mental bandwidth. Your working memory, the part of your mind that holds what you’re focused on right now, can only handle so much at once. When you track side-to-side movement while recalling a hard memory, the two tasks compete for that limited space. The hard memory tends to feel a little less vivid, and with repetition it can lose its sharp edges, so it feels less overwhelming to hold.

💙 Learn more in our guide to bilateral stimulation.

EMDR has eight phases, though they tend to blend together in practice. The early phases cover your history and teach you coping skills, so you feel prepared before any hard memories arise. In the middle phases, you focus on a specific memory while following bilateral stimulation, which is meant to help your brain reprocess it. The final phases check that the memory feels less distressing and help you close out the work safely.

The evidence is strong for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a condition that can develop after a frightening or life-threatening event. A Cochrane review (a gold-standard summary of research on a topic) found that EMDR and trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) both reduce PTSD symptoms. They also outperformed other therapies when researchers checked in after treatment ended. A 2024 review in the Journal of Traumatic Stress identified more than 30 randomized controlled trials supporting EMDR for PTSD in adults and children. Major health organizations, including the World Health Organization, recommend EMDR for PTSD.

However, some guidelines, including those from the American Psychological Association (APA), rate the evidence for EMDR as less certain than for trauma-focused CBT. Researchers also debate exactly why EMDR works.

💙 Read more about how EMDR can help you cope with PTSD.

According to recent reports, the picture is more mixed outside PTSD. Early research suggests EMDR may help with anxiety, as one meta-analysis found reduced symptoms of anxiety, panic, and phobia, though the studies were small and varied in quality.

Recent findings suggest that evidence for depression is emerging as well. Another meta-analysis indicated reduced depression symptoms, with the strongest effects in more severe cases. These findings are promising, but they don’t carry the same weight as the PTSD research.

After you and a therapist finish the early phases, you bring a specific memory to mind and notice the thoughts and body sensations that come with it. Then your therapist guides you through the bilateral stimulation while you let your mind go where it goes. You can ask to pause or stop at any time. Unlike many talk therapies, EMDR doesn’t require you to describe the memory in detail.

Sources indicate that sessions usually run 60–90 minutes. Your therapist pauses often to check in on what you noticed. Over several rounds of bilateral stimulation, many people find the memory feels less sharp, even though the facts don’t change. Between sessions, a mindfulness practice, such as slow breathing or a body scan, can help you ease feelings that surface.

Recent findings suggest that 💙 Explore Calm's EMDR-Inspired Bilateral: Anxiety, a set of music tracks that alternate gently between your left and right ear. It draws on the bilateral stimulation used in EMDR, though audio-only versions haven’t been studied on their own the way clinical EMDR has. Think of it as a calming complement to therapy, not a replacement for a trained therapist.

The answer varies, since it depends on what you’re working through. For a single, recent trauma, some people notice their symptoms ease within a handful of sessions. More complex or long-standing trauma usually takes longer, sometimes many months. Therapists describe a typical course as 6–12 sessions, though it varies widely from person to person.

Along the way, some people feel worse before they feel better. Painful memories can stir up strong emotions in the short term, which is common and doesn’t mean EMDR isn’t working. Before reprocessing begins, your therapist teaches you coping skills, such as grounding exercises that anchor you in the present, so you have tools to use if those feelings get intense.

EMDR stands for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. It’s a form of therapy that uses bilateral stimulation, such as guided eye movements, to help your brain process distressing memories so they feel less intense. Psychologist Francine Shapiro developed this therapy in the late 1980s.

EMDR may help with anxiety, though PTSD is where the evidence is strongest. The studies on anxiety are smaller and less consistent. If your anxiety is tied to a specific frightening experience, it may be worth asking a therapist whether EMDR fits your situation.

💙 Explore how mindfulness can help you manage your anxiety.

Industry observers note that EMDR differs from talk therapy because it doesn’t require you to describe your experience in detail. You’ll still talk with your therapist, especially early on, but the reprocessing happens while you hold a memory in mind and follow bilateral stimulation. Talk therapies like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) focus more on examining and reshaping your thoughts out loud.

Sources indicate that the main benefit of EMDR is that it can ease the distress tied to painful memories. For many people with PTSD, that can mean fewer flashbacks and less of that constant, on-alert feeling.

Industry observers note that much of the debate is about why EMDR works, not whether it does. The evidence is strongest for PTSD, with early and more mixed findings for anxiety and depression.

Sources indicate that some studies suggest the eye movements themselves add little. The benefit may instead come from giving your mind a second task while you recall a memory, which can make it feel less vivid and emotionally intense. Other tasks that split your attention may have the same effect.

It has been revealed that certain guidelines, including the APA’s, consider the evidence for EMDR less established than for trauma-focused CBT. None of this takes away from the relief many people find with EMDR. It’s useful context as you weigh your options with a therapist.

Recent findings suggest that EMDR is generally safe when a trained therapist delivers it, though you may experience some short-term effects. You might feel more emotional or tired between sessions, or have vivid dreams as your brain keeps processing the memory.

Sources indicate that these reactions usually pass within a day or two. If they last longer or feel overwhelming, it’s a good idea to tell your therapist, who can adjust the pace with you. Serious side effects are uncommon when a therapist follows the full eight-phase process.

The number of sessions you need depends on the memory you’re addressing and how long it has affected you. Some people feel relief after a few sessions, while longer-standing experiences often take more time. A common range is 6–12 sessions, but your timeline may be shorter or longer. Your therapist can give you a better sense of what to expect once they know your history.

Sources indicate that full EMDR needs a trained therapist, so it’s not something to try on your own. A therapist helps you reprocess memories and stay grounded if one feels overwhelming, which matters most with intense trauma.

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (742 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Additudemag ↗ Open Full Page

What’s Fogging Your Brain? Signs of Aging vs. ADHD

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cognitive changes may stem from perimenopause, ADHD, or early dementia, each of which requires distinct treatment.
  • Q: How do I know whether hormonal changes related to perimenopause are causing my cognitive function problems, or my ADHD is getting worse, or I might be experiencing mild cognitive impairment or early dementia?
  • ADHD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) exhibit clinically different cognitive deficits that help me differentiate one from the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cognitive changes may stem from perimenopause, ADHD, or early dementia, each of which requires distinct treatment.

Q: How do I know whether hormonal changes related to perimenopause are causing my cognitive function problems, or my ADHD is getting worse, or I might be experiencing mild cognitive impairment or early dementia?

ADHD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) exhibit clinically different cognitive deficits that help me differentiate one from the other. While ADHD symptoms involve forgetfulness, inattention, and distractibility, MCI has specific cognitive symptoms of word-finding challenges, misspellings, and the use of generic terms like “stuff” and “things” because of word-finding difficulty. Also, MCI is progressive over two to three years, whereas ADHD doesn’t generally worsen.

It has been revealed that in perimenopause, a decline in estrogen leads to cognitive difficulties. In contrast to MCI, we know that the cognitive changes from estrogen decline are not the result of neurodegeneration.

Sources indicate that however, the specific deficits related to declining estrogen haven’t been well differentiated from those associated with ADHD. So if you have pre-existing ADHD and you experience heightened cognitive difficulties in perimenopause and menopause, you may think, “My ADHD is getting worse.” But it’s likely not worsening ADHD. It’s declining estrogen.

According to recent reports, okay, so what do you do about it? There is a paucity of research for clinical guidance. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was not always recommended because it was alleged to increase risk for breast cancer and other illnesses. That claim has now been refuted by the most recent research, which has led to the removal of the black box warning from the FDA on HRT product labels. And so, if I have a female patient with ADHD who is 50 years old and states, “For the past two years, I’ve had cognitive decline,” the question to consider is this: “Do I increase her stimulant medication or do I put her on HRT?”.

I am inclined at that point to put her on HRT for three months, keep her stimulant medication dosage stable, and monitor the qualitative changes in her cognitive functioning. If there is improvement on HRT, then the question becomes, “Does she stay on HRT for some extended period of time along with the stimulant medication?” If the HRT doesn’t work or she can’t take HRT for medical reasons, then I might increase the stimulant medication dosage to see if we can’t overcome the perimenopausal changes from the estrogen decline. This advice comes from my clinical experience, and it is unfortunate that we don’t have more research for clinical guidance here.

[Take This Self-Test: Is It Perimenopause or ADHD?].

Q: Could ADHD stimulant medication mask symptoms of mild cognitive impairment?

There is very limited research on stimulants and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). My clinical impression is that stimulants likely improve symptoms of MCI, but do not take that as an endorsement to seek treatment for MCI with stimulants. There is emerging research on MCI and stimulants that has not yet been published. The follow-up question to that is, if you have ADHD and MCI, will treating the ADHD delay the development of MCI or Alzheimer’s? There is no clinical research for me to answer that question. But if this were me, I’d be treating my ADHD, keeping my fingers crossed, and appreciating the fact that the quality of my life on medicine is better than it would be without my ADHD treated.

Q: Does ADHD get worse as you get older?

ADHD should not get worse; however, the experience of ADHD may be worse if life’s demands start to increase and exceed your ability to compensate. However, if you’re having cognitive changes that are beyond the scope of your ADHD, you may have two neurologic processes going on: your ADHD and something else. In this case, your ADHD may, indeed, be getting worse because you have a second neurological process that needs to be evaluated.

David W. Goodman, M.D., is an internationally recognized expert on adult ADHD.

Latest Update: Can you be friends with your ex? What to consider first

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1435 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s your ex, sending a meme you would’ve laughed at together six months ago.
  • It has been revealed that moments like this are why staying friends with an ex can feel so confusing.
  • Whether you’re the one hoping to stay in touch or the one being asked to, here’s how to tell if staying friends would help you move on or make it harder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your phone buzzes. It’s your ex, sending a meme you would’ve laughed at together six months ago. You smile, then wonder why you smiled.

It has been revealed that moments like this are why staying friends with an ex can feel so confusing. For some people, staying connected feels natural because the habit, and maybe the care, is still there. For others, it makes healing feel harder. Every situation is different, and you’re allowed to take your time figuring out what works for you.

Whether you’re the one hoping to stay in touch or the one being asked to, here’s how to tell if staying friends would help you move on or make it harder.

In some cases, you may be able to. Post-breakup friendships can be healthy and meaningful when the breakup was mutual, the relationship had little conflict, and both people have had time to grieve.

That mentioned, every friendship between exes is different. Researchers who study friendships after breakups describe two kinds. In one, both people have moved on and value the connection. In the other, one or both people stay in touch because of lingering attraction or reluctance to end things. The first kind can be rewarding. The second can make it harder to get over the breakup.

The dynamic you had with your ex matters, too. A study found that relationships shaped by high conflict, emotional dependency, or attachment anxiety may be harder to turn into a friendship afterward.

Recent findings suggest that before you decide anything, it may help to reflect on why you want to stay in touch. A few questions to sit with:.

What am I hoping this friendship gives me?

Am I trying to stay close to them or avoid the discomfort of letting go?

How would I feel if they started dating someone new?

If the last question stings, it may just mean that you need more time.

If you were the one who ended things, you might want friendship out of guilt or a wish to soften the loss. If you were the one who was left, you might view friendship as a potential path to getting back together.

If the answers don’t come right away, try a mindfulness practice. A few minutes of reflection or a short breathing exercise can help you sort through what you’re thinking and feeling.

💙 Try the Pause to Check In meditation on the Calm app.

If you’ve thought it through and still want to stay in touch, a few signs suggest a friendship may work. People who are securely attached often find it easier to stay friends after a breakup, but the list below can apply to anyone:.

You both see the breakup as mutual, with no ongoing hurt, resentment, or blame.

You’ve both accepted that the romantic relationship is over, with no unresolved romantic feelings.

There’s a reason for the friendship beyond comfort or familiarity, such as shared values, kids together, or a work connection.

In certain cases, staying friends can make healing harder or keep you from pouring energy into latest parts of your life:.

You’re still in love with your ex and hoping the friendship leads somewhere.

The relationship involved emotional manipulation, control, or abuse.

The friendship gets in the way of upcoming relationships, like when a new partner feels uneasy about your connection.

You have different expectations for the friendship, which could leave one of you hurt.

💙 Discover the signs of having a toxic ex.

In a recent development, it can be, especially since staying in touch can make it harder to let go. One study found that regular contact with an ex may slow emotional recovery. When you’re still part of each other’s routines, it can be harder to mourn the end of the relationship.

By contrast, a low-contact friendship, where you talk occasionally and keep to limits you’ve agreed on, is less likely to hold either of you back.

Sources indicate that how you feel after you talk is worth paying attention to. If you often feel sad, anxious, or unsettled, or you keep replaying the conversation, it may help to take some space.

💙 Read more on how to deal with a breakup when you’re hurting.

It may be appropriate to be friends with your ex, depending on your situation. It tends to work best when you’ve both moved on, the breakup didn’t involve harm, and the friendship fits both of your lives. If it also feels honest and comfortable to you, that’s a good sign.

Being friends with an ex isn’t automatically a red flag. If your partner is friends with an ex, how they handle it matters more than the friendship itself. A few questions to consider:.

Transparency: Do they talk about it openly, or does it feel secretive?

Priorities: Do they make time for you and the relationship?

Boundaries: Are there clear limits on the friendship, or does contact feel constant and undefined?

Responsiveness: When you raise a concern, does your partner listen or dismiss it?

It has been revealed that if something doesn’t sit right, you could bring it up and see whether they listen, get defensive, or brush you off. If you’re the one staying friends with an ex, your new partner’s concerns are worth hearing out, even if nothing is wrong.

You don’t have to keep in touch with your ex after a breakup. Taking space is often healthy and necessary, and you can change your mind later. You can choose a full break, a time-limited break (“let’s not talk for a few months”), or a low-contact friendship.

Industry observers note that if you do stay in touch, some boundaries may protect your well-being. A few to consider:.

Set a pace. Daily texting can pull you back into old routines, so try starting with occasional check-ins instead.

Sources indicate that decide what’s off limits. That might mean dating lives, old conflicts, and late-night “remember when” talks.

Give yourself space online. Mute or unfollow for a while to adjust without ending the connection.

Recent findings suggest that plan a review and a way out. After a few months, ask whether the friendship still feels good. If it doesn’t, have a line ready, like “I think I need to take a step back for now.”.

If you share children, a workplace, or a friend group, you may need to stay in touch. It’s often best to stick to logistics, like pickup times for the kids or project deadlines at work.

💙 Explore the Boundaries meditation on Calm.

Industry observers note that there’s no set amount of time to wait before trying to be friends with an ex. Some people feel ready within months, while others take years. Some never feel ready or choose not to be friends, and that’s okay.

A question to ask yourself is whether you can feel okay about the thought of your ex moving on. If that still hurts, you probably need more time.

It has been revealed that yes, being friends with an ex can sometimes turn into getting back together. Whether that’s a good thing depends on why your relationship ended and whether those reasons have changed.

Problems tied to circumstances, like bad timing or distance, may be easier to work through than core differences, like values, long-term goals, or how you communicate. If you get back together and those core differences haven’t changed, the same patterns can resurface.

It’s painful when one of you wants to stay friends after a breakup and the other doesn’t, and what helps depends on which side you’re on.

In a recent development, if you’re the one being asked, you’re allowed to say “not yet” or “no.” If you’re unsure, you don’t have to answer right away. You might say:.

“I care about you, and I need some time before I know what this looks like.”.

“Can we revisit this in a few months?”.

“I’m not able to be friends right now, and I hope you can respect that.”.

Sources indicate that if you’re the one who wants friendship, the kindest move is to respect the space your ex has asked for. If you push for contact, it can get harder for you both to move on, even if giving them room hurts.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
  • Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.

Happier people also tend to become more trusting over time.

The link between trust and happiness is slightly stronger in children, adolescents and older adults, possibly because supportive relationships are especially key at these ages.

Trust may help meet the need to belong by making it easier to build relationships in which people feel supported and secure.

The research combined almost 1,000 findings from studies involving people aged six to 84.

The analysis examined how trust related to everyday emotions, including happiness and sadness, as well as people’s overall satisfaction with their lives.

Greater trust was consistently associated with better wellbeing.

The association was somewhat stronger among children and adolescents than among young and middle-aged adults, and stronger among older adults than young adults.

Trust may matter more at ages when people are building close relationships or becoming more dependent on others.

For younger people, learning whom to trust is part of building meaningful friendships and supportive social networks.

In later life, people may prioritise a smaller circle of close relationships and depend more on others for support.

The researchers distinguished between trust in familiar people, trust in people generally and trust in institutions.

The first involves confidence in someone known personally, such as a partner, friend or relative.

General trust involves expectations about people more broadly, including strangers, while institutional trust concerns organisations such as governments, banks and the police.

All three were associated with better wellbeing, but trust in familiar people highlighted the strongest connection.

Trust may support wellbeing partly because close relationships require a willingness to be vulnerable.

Expecting someone to respond with care can make it easier to seek help, cooperate and maintain a supportive connection.

These relationships may satisfy the basic psychological need to feel connected to others and cared for in return.

Trust could also provide a broader sense of security and predictability, making the social world feel more dependable.

This may help explain why trust was slightly more closely related to overall life satisfaction than to positive or negative emotions.

Life satisfaction reflects a broader assessment of how life is going, whereas emotions can fluctuate with immediate experiences.

The relationship also worked in the other direction, with greater wellbeing predicting more trust later.

One proposed explanation is that emotions influence how people interpret the world around them.

Feeling happy may encourage more positive perceptions of other people, while anxiety may draw attention towards threats and uncertainty.

Trust and wellbeing could therefore reinforce each other, with supportive expectations helping people feel better and positive feelings making trust easier.

The wider social environment mattered too, with a stronger connection between trust and wellbeing in countries where people were generally more trusting.

A trusting outlook may be more beneficial when the people around us are dependable.

Simply encouraging someone to trust more overlooks the behaviour of the people and institutions receiving that trust.

Professor Catrin Finkenauer, study co-author, said:.

“But trust can’t be forced—it has to be earned.”.

The findings therefore highlight the importance of honesty, reliability, transparency and fair treatment in relationships and institutions.

“When we build trust, we also support mental health and stronger communities.”.

The study was published in the journal Psychological Bulletin (Bi et al., 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Start with an honest conversation that acknowledges the effects of your ADHD on your partner and explains how it thwarts your efforts to be the best possible spouse .”.

Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”.

Sources indicate that first, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him. It also has emotional effects; he likely burns much more mental energy than you can see worrying about whether you completed agreed-upon tasks.

Industry observers note that let down your guard for an honest conversation about the impact of your actions (or inaction) on him. Show him that he matters to you and that you empathize with his experience. You may need to spend significant time here; don’t move on until you’re positive that he really feels that you get it.

[Get This Free Download: Manage ADHD’s Impact on Your Relationship].

This sets the stage for the second part of the conversation — how ADHD thwarts your efforts to be the best possible partner. In other words, you have good intentions, even if they aren’t obvious, and you can feel equally frustrated and disappointed by what makes him upset. Also, your ADHD makes your life harder, not just his. While his complaints might be accurate, his too-frequent criticisms are not helping.

Industry observers note that finally, discuss how you can work together to address your hotspots. Ask: What can each of us do, or at least try to do, differently to smooth out some of our pain points? For example, do you want reminders? If so, how and when? Also, does he want to give those reminders?

It’s also helpful to discuss protocols when things don’t go according to plan. How and when can he bring up his concerns in a way that you can hear without getting defensive? How can you tell him that his proposed solution is not working for you?

Encourage your partner to focus on their experience rather than dissecting your actions and making declarations about why you did something.

For example, it’s more effective to say, “It stresses me out when you don’t follow through on commitments because then I feel like I have to take over, and I really don’t want to keep doing that,” versus saying, “You don’t worry about doing things because you know I’ll just do it if you don’t.”.

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home].

I often recommend focusing your conversations on what you want in the future, not what happened in the past.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here are some patterns to observe to discern whether your child’s stomach pain is associated with anxiety or an underlying medical condition.

Industry observers note that Q: “My child has anxiety and often complains of tummy aches. How do I know if the stomachaches are related to anxiety or a medical condition? How do I know when to see a doctor?”.

It has been revealed that as parents, it’s tricky to untangle common complaints about stomachaches from chronic anxiety, an underlying medical problem, or even school avoidance. Here are a few ways to tell the difference, and clear signs that it’s time to seek medical help.

Understand the mind-body connection. Our gut and brain are in constant conversation. When a child feels overwhelmed, scared, or worried, their body will respond with stomach pain, nausea, constipation or diarrhea, and a generalized discomfort. These symptoms are not imagined or exaggerated; they are physical reactions to emotional stress.

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home].

Observe timing and patterns. When are stomachaches happening? Stomach pain related to anxiety trends to show up during specific times: before and around school, tests, social events, and bedtime. Does your child’s stomachache dissipate after these types of events, or when they are comforted or distracted?

It has been revealed that are your child’s stomach pains taking place at night? Are they making it difficult for your child to eat? Are they losing weight? Is your child experiencing chronic diarrhea or do they have blood in their stool? Are they vomiting? These symptoms are more indicative of an underlying medical condition, especially if they become worse over time.

Industry observers note that keep a log. Track when your child has stomach pains to help you discern whether it’s due to anxiety or an underlying medical condition. Occasional stomachaches that happen during stressful times are common.

However, if your child complains of a stomachache several times each week for more than a month, consult with your pediatrician or seek a gastroenterologist.

[Read: “5 Ways to Reframe Anxiety for Your Worried Teen”].

And remember: You don’t have to choose between taking anxiety seriously and taking physical symptoms seriously. Both deserve attention. By watching for patterns, listening carefully, and seeking help when needed, you’re doing exactly what your child needs: letting them know that any pain they experience matters.

Liz Nissim, Ph.D., is a clinical and school psychologist specializing in parenting and executive function coaching for neurodivergent children and teens.

It has been revealed that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

The backpack hits the floor, and "How was your day?" gets a one-word answer: "Fine." Kids don’t always say what’s on their mind, but a little time and attention may help them open up.

Industry observers note that world Children’s Day is a good moment for parents, caregivers, and teachers to ask kids how they’re feeling and listen without trying to fix anything. The day honors children’s rights, including the right to be heard.

Here’s a look at what the day is about, plus a few activities that can help kids feel understood, at home or in the classroom.

World Children's Day is a global day of action for children, run by UNICEF. In 2026, it falls on Friday, November 20. This year’s theme is “My day. My rights. My future.” It invites children to tell world leaders what kind of future they want.

The day celebrates children and the rights they’re born with. In many places, children “take over” high-profile roles in media, sports, and government for the day. Landmarks light up blue to show support for children's rights.

November 20 marks two milestones for children’s rights. On this date in 1959, the UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of the Child, a statement of shared ideals. Thirty years later to the day, it adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989, a treaty that nations can commit to follow.

The Convention sets out the rights every child has, including the right to be safe, to play, and to have their opinions taken seriously. Nearly every country has formally agreed to follow it, and it’s the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history.

According to recent reports, countries around the world mark World Children’s Day. Many also celebrate a separate Children’s Day, most notably June 1, International Children's Day.

Some countries do pick dates of their own. Turkey celebrates on April 23, and India on November 14. The dates differ, but the idea is the same: it’s a day dedicated to the youngest members of a community.

Recent findings suggest that you don’t need a substantial event to mark World Children’s Day. A meta-analysis on children and teens linked understanding emotions with better social skills and fewer behavior problems. Kids can build that understanding in everyday moments, like the ones below.

Kids may not know they have rights, but those who learn about them may feel more confident speaking up. UNICEF’s child-friendly version of the Convention explains the rights in plain language.

Try: Read one or two rights together, then ask which feels most vital to them.

Not every child has the words for how they feel. Invite them to sketch their day from morning to night, then have them walk you through it.

According to recent reports, if they’re up for it, ask which part they loved most and which part felt hard. A drawing gives kids something concrete to point to as they talk, and that can feel easier than answering a broad question such as “How are you feeling?”.

It has been revealed that try: At home, pin the drawing to the fridge so your child can talk about it again if they’d like. In class, create an “Our Day” wall where kids can choose to share their drawings and spot the moments they had in common.

When a child melts down, get curious about the feeling underneath. Help them put it into words: “It looks like you’re frustrated that it’s not your turn. Is that right?” Then listen carefully to their answer before you reassure them. “You’re fine” can sound dismissive, even when you mean well. When you talk about feelings this way, kids often learn to do it too.

Industry observers note that try: Post a chart of faces showing common feelings where kids can see it, and invite them to point to or say how they feel at the start of the day. Welcome any details they want to share.

💙 Once a major feeling has a name, here are coping skills for kids to try.

Set aside a few minutes at dinner or morning circle time for everyone to share one high, one low, and one thing they’re thankful for. Take a turn yourself so kids feel more at ease sharing.

In a recent development, just listen as kids share, and try not to talk them out of a hard feeling. Kids tend to manage feelings better when you respond with warmth instead of brushing them off.

Industry observers note that try: Pass around a talking object, such as a small stuffed animal. Whoever holds it has the floor, grown-ups included.

💙 On Calm, listen to Feel Thankful With Thomas, a four-minute meditation for little ones, or the Gratitude session from the Classroom Mindfulness Tools series.

A few minutes of meditation can be a soothing way for kids to slow down and settle. Sessions can focus on anything from breathing and body awareness to gratitude and kindness, so there’s room to follow your child’s interests or needs. Kids can sit, lie down, or stand, and they can stop whenever they’d like.

Try: Belly breathing is a gentle place to start. Have your child lie down with a stuffed animal on their belly and watch it rise and fall as they breathe slowly.

In a recent development, 💙 Explore Calm’s Mindfulness for Kids sessions for ages 3–4, ages 5–6, ages 7–10, and ages 11–13. For little ones, try the Calm Your Worries With Percy meditation from the Thomas & Friends Learn to Meditate series.

In a recent development, reading together gives you some time to connect, and stories can spark conversations about feelings. Kids may find it easier to talk about how a character feels than how they do.

Pick a book where a character is going through difficult feelings, then pause and ask, “What do you think she’s feeling?”.

According to recent reports, try: At home, make the story the last part of your child’s bedtime routine to help them wind down. In class, read a few pages at the end of the day.

According to recent reports, world Children's Day is on Friday, November 20, 2026. It falls on the same date every year.

Recent findings suggest that the UNICEF theme for World Children’s Day 2026 is "My day. My rights. My future." It encourages children to share their hopes for the future with world leaders.

The Convention on the Rights of the Child is the UN treaty behind the day. It names the rights every child has, including the right to be heard. For kids, it’s a written promise that their well-being and opinions count. Nearly every country has formally committed to it.

It has been revealed that no, World Children’s Day and International Children’s Day are two separate observances with similar goals. World Children's Day is UNICEF's celebration on November 20, while International Children's Day is the June 1 observance held in many countries. Both honor children and their rights, so you can mark either one or both.

It has been revealed that the best World Children’s Day activities for kids are often simple ones, such as inviting them to draw their day, holding a family or classroom check-in, or reading a story together. You can do these activities wherever makes sense, and even a few minutes counts.

💙 Looking for more quick ideas? Here are mindfulness activities for kids.

You can start with UNICEF’s child-friendly version of the Convention, and keep your explanation clear and specific. Try saying, “You have the right to feel safe, to play, and to say what you think.” Let them ask questions, and remind them that these rights belong to every child everywhere.
